name: Scenario Generation
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Asking the Right People the Right Questions: Scenario Generation in ATAM
lesson.summary: Scenario generation is the ATAM step where stakeholders brainstorm concrete situations an architecture must handle, turning vague goals like scalable or secure into specific, testable stories.
lesson.body:
The Architecture Tradeoff Analysis Method, developed by the Software Engineering Institute at Carnegie Mellon, evaluates a software architecture by checking it against the quality goals that actually matter to the people who will build, operate, and depend on it. Scenario generation is the step where those goals get translated from slogans into specifics. Nobody disagrees that a blockchain platform should be secure or scalable in the abstract. The disagreements, and the design decisions, only become visible once secure and scalable are written as concrete situations with a trigger, an expected response, and a way to check whether the response actually happened.

Scenario generation depends directly on stakeholder analysis. A payments blockchain has miners or validators who care about block reward stability, exchanges who care about settlement finality, regulators who care about auditability, wallet developers who care about API stability, and everyday users who mostly care about their transaction going through without a large fee. Each stakeholder group, brought into the room during an ATAM evaluation, generates a different set of scenarios, because each group notices different failure modes. A validator worries about a scenario where a chain reorganization erases blocks they already built on. An exchange worries about a scenario where a double spend attempt succeeds during a brief network partition.

In practice, scenario generation is run as a facilitated brainstorm, often using sticky notes or a shared document, followed by a vote where each stakeholder gets a fixed number of votes to spend on the scenarios they think matter most. This voting step matters because a real evaluation might surface eighty or a hundred candidate scenarios, far more than a review team can analyze in the time available. Prioritization by vote surfaces the scenarios the assembled stakeholders collectively consider most consequential, which is not the same as the scenarios any single architect would have picked alone.

Consider a concrete blockchain example. During a scenario generation session for a new proof of stake network, participants might propose: a validator's node loses power during block production and must resync without a slashing penalty, a coordinated set of validators controlling one third of stake goes offline simultaneously, or a client software bug causes half the network to accept an invalid block. Each is a raw scenario, a plausible story rather than a formal specification. The next step, covered separately, refines the highest voted scenarios into quality attribute scenarios with the precise structure ATAM requires.

The value of scenario generation is that it forces disagreement into the open before a single line of architecture is judged. A blockchain team convinced their consensus algorithm is secure will, if scenario generation is done honestly, still have to sit and listen to an exchange stakeholder describe exactly the double spend scenario that keeps them up at night. Skipping this step, and letting architects generate scenarios from their own assumptions, is one of the most common ways an ATAM evaluation ends up confirming what the architects already believed rather than testing it.
